metadata.title: Small Pushes, Large Response: Resonance
metadata.register: formal, undergrad/grad audience, no casual narration
metadata.branding: none — unbranded, book content only, no channel/logo/handle

beats.narration_text: How can small, steady footsteps make a large bridge sway?
beats.new_visual_element: Portrait-only opening question card (title-styled, crimson underline).

beats.narration_text: When the Millennium Footbridge in London opened, pedestrians felt it sway, and people continuing to cross reinforced the swaying until the bridge had to be closed. How can small, steady footsteps drive such a large motion?
beats.new_visual_element: Top view of a footbridge over a river: grey deck between two green banks, small pedestrian dots walking across; the deck sways sideways with slowly growing amplitude. Label 'footbridge, top view'.

beats.narration_text: Every springy structure has a natural frequency, the frequency at which it oscillates on its own, with no driving force. A mass on a spring is the simplest example: displace it and release it, and it bounces at its natural frequency, f zero, slowly losing amplitude to damping.
beats.new_visual_element: The bridge gives way to a vertical spring hanging from a support bar with a blue mass. Released, the mass oscillates freely with slowly decaying amplitude; a chart beside it records the mass's height against time (time scrolling left). Label f_0.
beats.accumulated_scene_state: spring-mass rig, free decaying oscillation, scrolling position chart

beats.narration_text: Now drive it, moving the top of the spring up and down with a small amplitude. If the driving frequency is far from the natural frequency, the pushes fall out of step with the motion. Some add energy, others take it away, and the response stays small.
beats.new_visual_element: The support bar turns crimson and moves up and down with a small amplitude at 1.7 times f_0; the mass responds weakly, and the chart trace stays flat and small. Label f_drive = 1.7 f_0.
beats.accumulated_scene_state: rig driven off resonance, small response on chart

beats.narration_text: Tune the drive to the natural frequency. Now every push arrives in step with the motion, energy is transferred efficiently on every cycle, and the amplitude grows with each oscillation, limited only by damping. The drive is just as small as before.
beats.new_visual_element: Label changes to f_drive = f_0; the support's motion is unchanged in size, but the mass's oscillation grows cycle by cycle and the chart trace fans out into a widening envelope.
beats.accumulated_scene_state: rig driven at resonance, growing response, widening trace

beats.narration_text: That is resonance: a small driving force, applied at the natural frequency, producing a large response. Footsteps falling in step with a bridge's sway reinforce it in exactly the same way.
beats.new_visual_element: Held frame with the resonant oscillation still large; summary 'SAME PUSH, RIGHT TIMING'.
